transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming this evening. I'm Dr Hana Patel, and tonight I'd like to talk about healthy eating for busy people.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Many of you told us in the survey that you don't have time to cook. Nearly sixty per cent said they eat ready meals at least three times a week. Ready meals aren't always bad, but they often contain a lot of salt. A single meal can have more than half of the salt an adult should eat in a whole day. So my first piece of advice is to read the label. Choose meals with less than one gram of salt per hundred grams.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Second, think about breakfast. Some people skip it to save time, but research shows that people who skip breakfast often eat more snacks before lunch. A bowl of porridge takes just five minutes and keeps you full until midday. If you really don't have time in the morning, prepare it the night before and keep it in the fridge.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Third, drink more water. Many of us confuse thirst with hunger. Before you reach for a biscuit at four o'clock, try drinking a glass of water and wait ten minutes. You might find that you don't need the biscuit. Aim for around two litres of fluid a day, although tea and coffee count too.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Finally, let's talk about fruit and vegetables. The advice is five portions a day, and a portion is about the size of your fist. Frozen vegetables are just as healthy as fresh ones, because they are frozen soon after they are picked, and they are often cheaper. You can add a handful of frozen peas to almost any meal.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: I want to emphasise that you don't have to change everything at once. Pick one idea and try it for two weeks. I'll be around after the talk if you have questions, and there are free leaflets on the table by the door.
